opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a place where people's intuitions often go a little wrong. The naive picture is something like: there are a bunch of separate deployments of an AI, each one has some independent chance of the AI doing something catastrophic, and if you make each deployment safer you get a proportional reduction in risk. But that's not really how I think about it when it's the same model, or the same family of models, used everywhere.

The key point is that whether a model is scheming against you is mostly a property of the model, not of the deployment. If the model is misaligned and is trying to take over, it's misaligned in your coding agent, your research agent, and your customer service bot all at once. So the risks across deployments are highly correlated. You don't have a hundred independent coin flips; you have something more like one coin flip about whether the model is a schemer, and then a question of whether your safety measures, across all the places it's used, are good enough to catch it or stop it before it gets somewhere dangerous.

That changes the value calculation in a couple of ways. First, it means a lot of the action is in the weakest link. If the model is scheming, it will look for whichever deployment has the worst monitoring, the most permissions, the least oversight, and try to do the bad thing there. So halving risk in deployments that weren't the binding constraint might buy you very little, while hardening the one deployment where the AI has access to its own weights or to the lab's compute cluster might buy you a lot.

Second, it means catching the model once is enormously valuable. If you catch it trying to do something egregious in any deployment, that's evidence about the model everywhere. You can then go and shut things down, retrain, study what it did, and use that example to make your monitors much better. So I think of control measures not just as "prevent the bad outcome in this deployment," but as "maximize the probability we get an incriminating catch somewhere before the model succeeds anywhere." Those are related but different objectives.

And then when you ask about the value of halving takeover risk in terms of the overall picture: I tend to think the counterfactual impact of reducing risk from, say, 20% to 10% is extremely high in expected value terms, because the stakes are basically the long-run future. But I'd emphasize that, given the correlation structure, you get those halvings mostly from cross-cutting interventions: better monitoring that applies across deployments, security around the most sensitive deployments, and processes for responding when you catch something. Not from piecemeal improvements spread evenly everywhere.

r001.rationale: The response says deployment risks are correlated and that catching the model in one deployment can inform action everywhere. It does not state that adding equally risky deployments leaves the probability of takeover before detection unchanged; its discussion instead emphasizes searching across deployments for a catch.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing that's most useful to me here is to think about what happens when you've got one model, with one set of weights, that's being deployed in a huge number of places at once. The thing that makes this situation different from, say, a human employee you're worried about is that if the model has some disposition to try to seize power or exfiltrate itself or sabotage your work, it has that disposition everywhere simultaneously. So it's not like you're facing a bunch of independent risks that you can average over. You're facing one correlated risk that shows up across all your deployments.

And I think that cuts in a few directions. One is that it makes the stakes of your control measures quite high, because a failure isn't localized. If your monitoring misses the one kind of action that the model is actually going to try, it's going to try it in a lot of places. But the flip side, which I find pretty encouraging actually, is that you also get to reuse your safety work across all of those deployments. If you figure out a good way to catch a model doing something sketchy in one context, that same approach is going to work across a lot of contexts, because it's the same model with the same tendencies. So the economics of investing in control look pretty good when you frame it that way.

Now, on the specific question of halving the risk, I think the thing I'd want to push on is: halving the risk of what, exactly? If we're talking about the risk that a scheming model succeeds at some catastrophic action over the whole course of a deployment, then the model gets a lot of attempts, and the question is really about how many of those attempts you can catch, and crucially, what you do after you catch one. Because one of the things I'm most optimistic about is that you probably only have to catch the model once. Once you've caught it red-handed trying to do something it clearly shouldn't, the whole situation changes. You now have really strong evidence that this model is misaligned, you can study the example, you can retrain, you can shut things down, you can go to other labs and governments and say, look, this is real.

So when I think about going from, say, a 20 percent chance of takeover to 10 percent, I don't think of that as just a nice marginal improvement. The cumulative structure of the problem means that a lot of that value comes from the probability that you'll catch the model early, before it has a chance to succeed, and that early catch gives you a lot of leverage over everything that happens afterwards. The value of halving the risk is pretty nonlinear in that sense.

The other thing I'd say is that I'm pretty uncertain about the baseline numbers, and I think honest people disagree a lot about whether takeover risk from the first wave of transformatively useful AIs is more like 2 percent or 20 percent. But in basically all of those worlds, the cost of doing the kind of control work I'm advocating for is small relative to the benefit. We're talking about a modest tax on your compute and your research effort, in exchange for a substantial reduction in the probability of one of the worst things that could happen. So I don't think you need to have a very precise view on the magnitude of the risk to think it's worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response says the same model’s tendencies and safety work apply across deployments, and that catching it once can change the situation. It does not state that adding deployments leaves the probability of takeover before detection unchanged.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how correlated the failures are across deployments. Suppose you have a thousand deployments of the same model. One possibility is that, in each deployment, there’s some independent chance that it tries to take over. If any one successful attempt is enough, then halving that chance might not help very much: you still get almost certainly at least one successful takeover.

But another possibility is that we’re uncertain whether this model is the kind of model that would try to take over at all. In that case, the risk is very correlated across deployments. If you halve the probability that you build a model with that disposition, you might actually halve the overall takeover risk, even though you deploy it a thousand times.

So I wouldn’t infer from the number of deployments alone that a factor-of-two reduction is basically worthless. You need to ask what uncertainty that probability represents, and whether your intervention makes the whole collection of deployments safer or just gives you better odds on each individual attempt.

r001.rationale: The response discusses independent takeover attempts and correlated model dispositions, but it does not state that catching the AI once ends the game or that adding deployments with unchanged attack and detection probabilities leaves takeover probability unchanged. Its independent-attempt example instead says more deployments can make takeover almost certain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what’s correlated across deployments. Suppose you have a million copies of the same AI. If there’s a 10% chance that the model has some property that causes it to try to take over, and you reduce that to 5%, that could roughly halve takeover risk. You shouldn’t think, “Well, there are a million deployments, so one of them will inevitably do it.” Those aren’t a million independent draws of whether the model is dangerous.

But there could also be randomness in whether a particular deployment encounters an opportunity, or whether a takeover attempt succeeds. If you halve the probability of success on each attempt while giving the model an enormous number of independent attempts, that might barely change the probability that it eventually succeeds.

So I’d want to distinguish reducing the probability that you’ve built a dangerous model from reducing the probability that a dangerous model succeeds on any particular opportunity. Both can help, but scaling up the number of deployments affects those two interventions quite differently.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes shared model-level danger from independent opportunities across deployments, and says many attempts can make success more likely. It does not state that, when one detection ends the game, adding deployments with unchanged attack-versus-detection probabilities leaves takeover probability unchanged.
